title: Places and journeys
job: A trip told in full, with directions inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Der Zug fährt um acht ab
Von dort + sind wir + zu Fuß + weitergegangen

rules.text: DIRECTION IS MARKED ON THE QUESTION WORD, and English has no category for it. One English where does three jobs; German splits them. wo asks about a static place (L1-M7's), wohin asks where TO, woher asks where FROM. They are three separate words to learn, not variants of one — and a learner who asks Wo gehen Sie? has asked a question German does not ask.

hin POINTS AWAY FROM THE SPEAKER, her POINTS TOWARDS THEM. They attach to the front of a question word — wohin, woher — and to the back of a place word — dorthin, hierher. In speech they can also break off and go to the end of the clause: Wo wollen Sie hin? is the same question as Wohin wollen Sie? Getting hin and her the right way round is what makes a journey sentence sound German.

GERMAN HAS THREE WAYS TO SAY to AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. nach for countries, cities and Hause. zu for a person, a shop, a named building. in plus the ACCUSATIVE for going INTO something — ins Kino, in die Stadt. English has one word for all three, so an anglophone picks by feel and is wrong about a third of the time. All three German words are already yours from lower rungs — nach is L2-M4's, in is L1-M1's, and L1-M8's zu is the too of zu teuer rather than a preposition at all — so this is a choice to make, not a word to learn.

THE VEHICLE TAKES mit AND THE DATIVE: mit dem Bus, mit dem Zug, mit dem Auto. Walking takes no article at all — zu Fuß — and it is a fixed phrase rather than a pattern. English travel by has one preposition for both, and German has one preposition and one bare noun.

A SEPARABLE VERB STRANDS ITS PREFIX AND SOMEBODY HAS TO OWN IT. abfahren splits — Der Zug fährt um acht ab — and the ab left at the end is a word in its own right. L3-M1 wrote such verbs and did not open the prefix; this module does, because a timetable sentence cannot avoid it. The same ab is also the plain preposition of ab Montag, from Monday on: one word, two seats, exactly as L1-M4's auf works.

THE DIRECTIONS THEMSELVES ARE ALREADY YOURS. links, rechts, geradeaus, Ecke, Ampel, einsteigen, aussteigen, ankommen and abfahren all belong to L2-M4, and the two-way prepositions with their accusative-or-dative rule belong there too. This module does not restate any of it — it is where that rule finally pays, inside one continuous account instead of one exchange at a corner.

sentences.display: Wohin fahren Sie? Wir machen einen kleinen Ausflug
sentences.cue: Where are you going? We are taking a short trip
sentences.literal: Where-to travel you? We make a small excursion

words.note: The question word for a destination. wo asks where something IS; wohin asks where it is going, and the two are never swapped.
Masculine: der Ausflug. Short and for pleasure — a Reise is longer, and you MAKE an Ausflug: einen Ausflug machen.

sentences.trap: English asks where are you going with the same where as where are you. German cannot: a destination needs wohin, and wo here would be a different question.
sentences.sound: voh-HIN FAA-run zee? veer MAKH-un EYE-nun KLY-nun OWS-flook.

variations.display: Wo wollen Sie hin? Wir machen einen kleinen Ausflug
variations.cue: Where do you want to go? We are taking a short trip
variations.changed: wohin split in two: wo stays in front and hin goes to the end. This is what people actually say.

mistake.display: Wo fahren Sie? Wir machen einen kleinen Ausflug
mistake.why: Wo fahren Sie? asks where the driving is happening, which is not a question anybody asks. A destination takes wohin.

sentences.usage: Making conversation with somebody who is clearly on their way somewhere.
sentences.mnemonic: wo stands still; wohin sets off.

sentences.display: Woher kommt der Zug, und in welche Richtung fährt er?
sentences.cue: Where does the train come from, and which direction does it go in?
sentences.literal: Where-from comes the train, and in which direction travels it?

words.note: The origin question, and it swallows the from: Woher kommen Sie? never takes a von in front of it.
Feminine, like every noun in -ung: die Richtung. in welche Richtung takes the accusative, because it is a direction.
The third person of L1-M6's fahren, and the a takes an umlaut: ich fahre but er fährt. Same vowel change as schlafen and tragen.

sentences.trap: Woher already means from where, so von woher is one from too many. The preposition is inside the word.
sentences.sound: voh-HAIR komt dair tsook, oont in VEL-khuh RIKH-toong fairt air?

variations.display: Woher kommen Sie? Und in welche Richtung gehen Sie?
variations.cue: Where do you come from? And which direction are you going in?
variations.changed: The same two questions asked of a person instead of a train; woher does not change its shape for either.

mistake.display: Von woher kommt der Zug, und in welche Richtung fährt er?
mistake.why: woher is already where-from. Adding von in front of it doubles the preposition, which is the English from where carried straight across.

sentences.usage: At a platform, working out whether this is the right train.
sentences.mnemonic: woher brings the from with it.

sentences.display: Der Zug fährt um acht ab und kommt um zehn an
sentences.cue: The train leaves at eight and arrives at ten
sentences.literal: The train travels at eight off and comes at ten on

words.note: Two seats, one word. It is the stranded prefix of abfahren — fährt … ab — and the plain preposition of ab Montag, from Monday on.

sentences.trap: The prefix is at the far end of the clause, so the sentence only means leaves once you have reached ab. Reading German timetables means reading to the end.
sentences.sound: dair tsook fairt oom akht AP oont komt oom TSAYN AN.

variations.display: Ab Montag fährt der Zug um neun
variations.cue: From Monday the train goes at nine
variations.changed: The other seat: ab as a plain preposition of time, in first position, with no verb to be a prefix of.

mistake.display: Der Zug abfährt um acht und ankommt um zehn
mistake.why: In a main clause a separable verb splits: the stem takes second position and the prefix goes last. Keeping it whole is what a subordinate clause does.

sentences.usage: Reading a departure board out loud to somebody.
sentences.mnemonic: The prefix waits at the end of the sentence, like the guard on the platform.

sentences.display: Wo wollen Sie hin? Kommen Sie bitte her!
sentences.cue: Where do you want to go? Come here, please!
sentences.literal: Where want you to? Come you please hither!

words.cue: there, away (direction away from the speaker)
words.note: Points away from whoever is speaking. It rides on the front of wohin or the back of dort — dorthin — or stands at the end of its own clause.

words.cue: here, this way (direction towards the speaker)
words.note: The mirror of hin: towards the speaker. hierher is to this spot, and Kommen Sie her is the whole of come here.

sentences.trap: English here and there say where something is. hin and her say which way it is moving, and neither one names a place at all.
sentences.sound: voh VOL-un zee HIN? KOM-un zee BIT-uh HAIR.

variations.display: Wollen Sie dorthin? Nein, ich möchte hierher
variations.cue: Do you want to go there? No, I would like to come here
variations.changed: The bare adverbs joined to their place words: dort plus hin, hier plus her. The direction is the second half of each.

mistake.display: Wo wollen Sie her? Kommen Sie bitte hin!
mistake.why: The two are the wrong way round. A destination takes hin and a summons towards the speaker takes her — swapping them reverses the journey.

sentences.usage: Sorting out, at a busy corner, who is going which way.
sentences.mnemonic: hin goes hence; her comes here.

sentences.display: Wir fahren mit dem Bus und gehen dann zu Fuß weiter
sentences.cue: We are going by bus and then carrying on on foot
sentences.literal: We travel with the bus and go then to foot further

words.note: Fixed, and it takes no article at all: zu Fuß gehen. Every other means of travel takes mit plus the dative — mit dem Bus.

sentences.trap: English by covers both halves of this sentence — by bus, on foot. German uses mit plus a dative for one and a bare two-word phrase for the other.
sentences.sound: veer FAA-run mit daym boos oont GAY-un dan tsoo FOOS VY-ter.

variations.display: Wir fahren mit dem Zug und gehen dann zu Fuß weiter
variations.cue: We are going by train and then carrying on on foot
variations.changed: Bus becomes Zug and the dative dem does not move: the vehicle changes, the frame does not.

mistake.display: Wir fahren mit dem Bus und gehen dann zu dem Fuß weiter
mistake.why: zu Fuß is frozen and takes no article. Expanding zu into zu dem turns a set phrase into a sentence about walking towards a foot.

sentences.usage: Explaining how you plan to cover the last part of a journey.
sentences.mnemonic: The bus takes a dative; the feet take nothing.

sentences.display: In Berlin müssen Sie umsteigen und weiter nach München fahren
sentences.cue: In Berlin you have to change and travel on to Munich
sentences.literal: In Berlin must you change and further to Munich travel

words.note: The third of L2-M4's steigen family: einsteigen on, aussteigen off, umsteigen across. Split, the bare stem stands alone: Wir steigen um.
Carrying on with what you were doing: weiter fahren, weiter gehen. It goes in front of the verb it extends.

sentences.trap: nach München, not zu München. A city always takes nach; zu is for a person or a named building.
sentences.sound: in ber-LEEN MUE-sun zee OOM-shty-gun oont VY-ter naakh MUEN-khun FAA-run.

variations.display: In Berlin steigen wir um und fahren weiter nach München
variations.cue: In Berlin we change and travel on to Munich
variations.changed: Without the modal, umsteigen splits: steigen second, um at the end of its clause.

mistake.display: In Berlin müssen Sie umsteigen und weiter zu München fahren
mistake.why: zu is for a person, a shop or a named building. Cities and countries take nach, and München is a city.

sentences.usage: Passing on what a ticket office just told you.
sentences.mnemonic: nach a place on the map, zu a place with a door.

sentences.display: Wir waren lange unterwegs und kamen erst spät zurück
sentences.cue: We were on the road a long time and only got back late
sentences.literal: We were long on-the-way and came only late back

words.cue: on the way, on the road, out and about
words.note: One word, and it never takes an article. It covers the whole of being between two places, however you are travelling.
Direction, not place: zurück is the way back. It goes at the end of the clause, where a separable prefix would.

sentences.trap: erst here is L4-M1's not until, not first. kamen erst spät zurück says we did not get back until late, and there is no other event it is first of.
sentences.sound: veer VAA-run LANG-uh oon-ter-VAYKS oont KAA-mun airst shpayt tsoo-RUEK.

variations.display: Wir sind lange unterwegs gewesen und kamen spät zurück
variations.cue: We were on the road a long time and got back late
variations.changed: waren becomes the spoken Perfekt sind … gewesen; the Präteritum kamen stays, because a written account mixes both.

mistake.display: Wir waren lange unterwegs und kamen zurück erst spät
mistake.why: zurück closes the clause, so nothing follows it. Time and manner go in front of it, exactly as they go in front of a separable prefix.

sentences.usage: Explaining a late arrival the next morning.
sentences.mnemonic: unterwegs is between; zurück is the end of the line.

sentences.display: Die Reise ging über eine Brücke und einen kleinen Fluss
sentences.cue: The journey went over a bridge and a small river
sentences.literal: The journey went over a bridge and a small river

words.note: Feminine: die Reise. The long one — a holiday or a crossing — where an Ausflug is out and back in a day.
Feminine: die Brücke. über eine Brücke is accusative, because crossing it is a direction, not a place.
Masculine: der Fluss, with a short u and the ss that a short vowel demands. The plural takes the umlaut: die Flüsse.

sentences.trap: über takes the accusative here because the journey crosses the bridge. Standing on it would be über der Brücke, and only the case says which.
sentences.sound: dee RY-zuh ging UE-ber EYE-nuh BRUE-kuh oont EYE-nun KLY-nun FLUS.

variations.display: Die Reise ging über einen Berg und einen kleinen Fluss
variations.cue: The journey went over a mountain and a small river
variations.changed: Brücke becomes Berg, so the article changes with the gender: eine Brücke against einen Berg.

mistake.display: Die Reise ging über einer Brücke und einem kleinen Fluss
mistake.why: Dative would place the journey on top of the bridge without moving. Crossing is a direction, so über takes the accusative.

sentences.usage: Recounting the shape of a route to somebody who does not know it.
sentences.mnemonic: Crossing takes the accusative; standing takes the dative.

sentences.display: Von dort sind wir zu Fuß auf den Berg gegangen
sentences.cue: From there we walked up the mountain
sentences.literal: From there are we to foot onto the mountain gone

words.cue: there (a place away from both of us)
words.note: The far there, where L2-M7's da is the near or vaguer one. Add hin for the direction: dorthin.
Masculine: der Berg. Going up one is auf den Berg — accusative, because it is a direction, and the dative would be standing on it.

sentences.trap: gehen with sein in the Perfekt is L2-M10's rule and it is still true here: any movement from one place to another takes sind, never haben.
sentences.sound: fon DORT zint veer tsoo FOOS owf dayn bairk guh-GANG-un.

variations.display: Von dort sind wir zu Fuß in die Stadt gegangen
variations.cue: From there we walked into town
variations.changed: auf den Berg becomes in die Stadt: a different two-way preposition, the same accusative, because both are destinations.

mistake.display: Von dort haben wir zu Fuß auf den Berg gegangen
mistake.why: gehen is a verb of movement, so its Perfekt takes sein: sind gegangen. haben here is the English have walked translated word for word.

sentences.usage: The middle of a story about a day out.
sentences.mnemonic: dort is over there; dorthin is on the way over there.

sentences.display: Haben Sie eine Karte? Ich finde den Weg zum Meer nicht
sentences.cue: Do you have a map? I cannot find the way to the sea
sentences.literal: Have you a map? I find the way to-the sea not

words.note: Feminine: die Karte. One word for a map, a postcard and a ticket — the context does all the work.
Masculine: der Weg, with a long e. Do not read it as the adverb weg (away), which has a short one.
Neuter: das Meer, and ans Meer fahren is what a German holiday does. See is a lake, and it is a different word.

sentences.trap: German says I find the way not where English says I cannot find it. The negation alone carries the failure — no modal is needed.
sentences.sound: HAA-bun zee EYE-nuh KAR-tuh? ikh FIN-duh dayn vayk tsoom MAIR nikht.

variations.display: Haben Sie eine Karte? Ich finde den Weg zum Bahnhof nicht
variations.cue: Do you have a map? I cannot find the way to the station
variations.changed: Meer becomes Bahnhof: both are neuter or masculine with dem, so zum covers them both unchanged.

mistake.display: Haben Sie eine Karte? Ich kann den Weg zum Meer nicht finden
mistake.why: Not wrong, but heavier than German needs. Ich finde … nicht is what a person actually says; the modal is the English cannot showing through.

sentences.usage: Asking a stranger for help when you are already lost.
sentences.mnemonic: der Weg is long; weg is gone.
